Visiting the website
The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. Hosting providers may process request information to serve pages and maintain their services. This version of the site does not load Google Analytics.

title: Privacy
text:
Subscriptions and comments
The optional subscription form sends your email address to the site’s subscription service. A confirmation email is used to verify your subscription. The comment form sends your chosen name and comment text to the site’s comment service. Approved comments may appear publicly, so please avoid including private information in a comment.
These features use Supabase and Cloudflare Turnstile. Turnstile checks help protect submissions from spam. On blog pages, a browser-local identifier is stored for the interaction features.
You can read the providers’ information at GitHub, Supabase, and Cloudflare.

About me

  
  
    
      Earth system science and artificial intelligence
      PhD programme at PolyU, jointly supervised with EIT
      Background in water engineering and groundwater science
      Research on weather, water, and ocean forecasting
      Interested in physically interpretable AI
    
  


I am LUO Qun (罗群). My work connects Earth system science with artificial intelligence, with a particular interest in physically interpretable prediction.
My background is in groundwater science and water engineering. I have worked on river water quality, precipitation nowcasting, human influences on runoff, and seasonal ocean forecasting. Across these topics, I am interested in how models can make useful predictions while helping us understand the processes behind them.

title: LUO Qun · 罗群
text:
Precipitation nowcasting




How can different forecasting approaches work together?




I investigated strategies for coupling deep learning and optical flow in satellite-based precipitation nowcasting over China.




The study compares the performance of different coupling strategies across regions and forecast lead times.




This work was published in Hydrological Sciences Journal in 2026, following online publication in 2025. Read the paper · Explore the code.

title: LUO Qun · 罗群
text:
Learning across a river network




Can information from one part of a river help predict another?




I studied water quality prediction in Beijing’s sub-center using LSTM and back-propagation neural networks.




The transfer-learning approach uses the upstream–downstream relationships between river gauges.




The work was published in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2023. Read the paper.

title: LUO Qun · 罗群
text:
From hydrology to ocean forecasting




My research in 2024–2025 explored the effects of human activities and climate change on runoff.




At the Southern University of Science and Technology, I have worked on deep learning for seasonal sea surface temperature forecasting, with related interests in algal bloom drivers and prediction.




These directions connect to my broader interest in physically interpretable AI for Earth system processes.












Project Collaborators
My water quality and precipitation research was conducted with Prof. Dingzhi Peng and collaborators at Beijing Normal University. The complete author lists are available on the publications page.
At Southern University of Science and Technology, my research experience is with Dr. Zhenzhong Zeng and the Earth System & Global Change Lab.
My PhD programme in Computing at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, starting September 2026, is jointly supervised with EIT, with Prof. Jiannong Cao and Dr. Yuntian Chen.

title: What To Do in the Era of Automated Research
text: This is the first post on my rebuilt personal website. It is intentionally short and a bit raw: a snapshot of what I have been thinking about most recently.

title: What To Do in the Era of Automated Research
text:
Questions I keep returning to

Can automated research workflows change how we choose questions, not just how we answer them?
What should we do (practically, ethically, career-wise) during this transition period?
Where do we position ourselves in the AI era: tool builders, tool users, reviewers, field scientists, theorists, or translators between them?
What is still meaningful work in the 21st century when “output” becomes cheap?




An example of a fully automated research workflow: AI-Scientist-v2 by Sakana AI.



The meaning of research is not to make research meaningless.
Our mission is to locate ourselves honestly within each stage of a field’s development.

The essence of scientific research is turning the unknown into reliable knowledge. In practice, it is a human process of generating new, reasonable, and useful claims on top of what we already know.
Most fields still share a similar loop:

Study the literature and context
Find a question worth asking
Form a hypothesis (or a model of what might be true)
Design experiments/observations and collect evidence
Analyze, interpret, and draw conclusions
Write (paper, code, lab notes) and publish/review
Communicate, reflect, and iterate

Now ask yourself: which parts can you do better than AI today, and which parts could you do better after learning to work with AI well?
My current answer is: taste and judgment still matter most. Not only “scientific taste”, but also the ability to sense what different audiences need and value, and to translate between them.
One framing I like is:

To P (peers): rigorous contributions that hold up under scrutiny
To B (business): reliable systems that create measurable value
To C (clients/users): solutions that reduce friction and fit real workflows
To H (humans): meaning, trust, and a sense of direction

Automation may replace many research processes, but “what counts as excellent research” is not fixed. It changes over time, and it also becomes a moving target for AI training. That is exactly where we should learn to stand: defining goals, updating standards, and staying honest about trade-offs.
To make work meaningful, we still need to do the basics well at each stage and in each role. Here is a simple metaphor:

As an advisor: keep strategic control.
AI can optimize processes toward a goal, but it cannot decide the ultimate goal over the long term.
As a general: turn strategy into workable tactics.
AI can help refine steps, but humans still need to translate high-level aims into operational plans.
As a soldier: execute with discipline.
As a researcher, building a reliable workflow for your own field is urgent and personal: no one understands your constraints better than you.
